Typography: what an engine owes a sentence

Good typesetting is invisible: the reader sees words, not the machinery that spaced them. This fixture exercises the passes that earn that invisibility — real shaping, total-fit line breaking, justified glue, hyphenation, and the optical niceties of protrusion and expansion. Compare the texture of these paragraphs against a first-fit engine: the spaces are uniform, no river runs down the column, and punctuation hangs neatly into the margins instead of being trapped inside the box, as if the typesetter had set the page by hand, line by line, the way a careful printer would.

Consider how a justified line is made: every inter-word space carries a natural width plus a little stretch and a little shrink, and the line's excess or deficit is distributed across those spaces in proportion — never one giant gap at the end of the line, never a crammed seam between two words. When the spaces run out of room, the engine may expand the glyphs themselves, by a hair, within two percent; you cannot see it, but the line now reaches the margin exactly, and the next line begins where the last one ended, and the column edge is straight as a ruled line, on the left and on the right, on every page, from the first paragraph to the last.

Punctuation is where the difference shows: a period at the end of a justified line is a tiny mark with a great deal of white around it, so it hangs slightly into the margin — a comma, a semicolon, a colon, a question mark, an exclamation point, each hangs by its own measure, determined once, applied everywhere. Open a book from a real press and hold a ruler to the right edge of the text block: the letters align, but the punctuation drifts past them, by a hair; that is protrusion, and now we do it too. Quotes at the start of a line hang the other way, into the left margin, so the opening mark never pushes the first letter off the grid. It is a small thing, but a page full of small things is a page that feels set, not dumped.

The whole craft rests on measurement: every word is shaped against the actual font before a single line is chosen, so the advances that decide where a line breaks are the advances the reader will see. A capital W is wide and an i is narrow, and the engine knows both, exactly, to a fraction of a point; it does not guess by counting letters. The lines below are broken by a dynamic program that considers the whole paragraph at once, trading a loose line here for a tight one there, so that the total cost across the paragraph — the sum of the spacing badness of every line, plus a penalty for each hyphen — is as small as the paragraph allows. That is the difference between filling a box and setting a paragraph, and it is why the texture of these words is even, from the top of the page to the bottom.

Hyphenation

When a long word will not fit, the engine may break it, politely, with a hyphen. Consider the celebrated word antidisestablishmentarianism, or its longer cousin pneumonoultramicroscopicsilicovolcanoconiosis: both are broken by Knuth-Liang patterns at the syllables English readers expect, never mid-morpheme, and each hyphen carries a cost, so the engine prefers a clean break between words and hyphenates only when it genuinely helps. The next paragraph disables hyphenation, and you can see the column edge roughen where the long word overflows, because a word that will not break must not be broken — it is set whole, at whatever cost to the margin, rather than sliced in ignorance.

Here the same words appear with hyphenation switched off: antidisestablishmentarianism and pneumonoultramicroscopicsilicovolcanoconiosis stay whole, and the right margin gives way to them, which is the honest behavior — an engine that guesses at syllable boundaries invents words, and an invented word is worse than an imperfect margin, every time, without exception, on any page of any document anyone will ever read, hyphenated or not, justified or not.

The small print

Everything here is deterministic: the same input, the same font bytes, and the same width produce the same glyphs, the same breakpoints, the same protrusion, and the same expansion, run after run, on every platform; the PDF that this document renders into is byte-for-byte identical every time you render it, which matters when a contract, a catalog, or a court filing must be reproduced exactly, with no drifting metrics, no re-shaped lines, and no surprise reflow between one print run and the next.

“The craft of typography is the craft of making the machinery disappear — of setting words so the reader meets the author, not the engine.” — after the printers of old
